#5495. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5494. Nationwide Equities debuts ReverseReach tool for mortgage broker lead generation help

Nationwide Equities has launched ReverseReach, a tool and help desk program that lets mortgage brokers and loan officers screen their existing customer databases for reverse mortgage opportunities without deep product expertise. The platform pairs a simple scenario runner with access to full-time underwriters, aiming to lower barriers to reverse lending and give originators a way to generate new business from past clients amid a challenging forward mortgage market.  AI Summary

Nationwide Equities Corp. has launched ReverseReach, a new tool and support program aimed at helping mortgage brokers and loan officers uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in their existing customer databases and referral networks, the company announced Tuesday.

The New Jersey-based wholesale reverse mortgage lender said ReverseReach is designed for originators who may not specialize in reverse products but have years of past customers who are now older, equity rich and potential candidates for reverse mortgages.

“Mortgage brokers may be sitting on substantial untapped business opportunities without even realizing it,” Paul Lamparillo, CEO of Nationwide Equities, said in a statement. “Over the years, brokers have built relationships with thousands of homeowners, many of whom may now qualify for reverse mortgage products.

“We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them.”

The company has largely pivoted to proprietary reverse mortgage production, mirroring recent changes in the broader industry. Modex data shows that Nationwide Equities has originated 111 reverse mortgages for $216 million in volume over the past 12 months, while data compiled by Reverse Market Insight shows that it has endorsed 26 Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) through the first nine months of this year.

In 2020, Nationwide Equities launched its private-label reverse mortgage, EquityPower, which was built to offer higher loan proceeds than HECM products.

ReverseReach allows mortgage professionals to enter a borrower’s financial and property scenario and quickly gauge whether a reverse mortgage is worth pursuing. The program is positioned as a preliminary opportunity identification tool rather than a full underwriting engine.

Regardless of the initial result, brokers can connect with a live underwriter to discuss the file and potential structures, according to the company.

Nationwide Equities is pairing the technology with a help desk staffed by full-time Direct Endorsement (DE) underwriters who answer eligibility questions, help structure loans and walk brokers through complex borrower situations.

“One of the biggest obstacles to broader reverse mortgage adoption is simply recognizing when a borrower may be a good candidate,” Philip Parziale, president of Nationwide Equities said in a statement. “ReverseReach bridges that gap. Brokers don’t need to become reverse mortgage experts to identify a potential transaction. They need a simple way to recognize the opportunity and a knowledgeable lending partner to help them execute it.”

Parziale added that direct access to underwriters is a central part of the offering. “Regardless of how good your technology is, there is something special about being able to speak to a live person on the phone and walk you through a scenario and respond to follow ups,” he said.

The launch comes as volume in the broader forward mortgage market remains under pressure from higher rates, tighter affordability and intense competition for a smaller pool of qualified borrowers. Many retail and broker shops are looking to diversify into reverse mortgages, home equity products or nonqualified mortgages (non-QM) to stabilize production.

For brokers, the reverse space has historically been constrained by product complexity, reputation concerns and training requirements. ReverseReach aims to lower that barrier by giving originators a simple screening workflow across their existing loan origination system and past client lists, backed by lender-side expertise.

Lenders are investing in education and simple tools to capture aging-in-place demand from older homeowners with significant home equity. Brokers who have closed thousands of loans over the past decade may find that a meaningful share of these clients now meet age and equity thresholds for reverse products.

#5493. LGI Homes Q3 2026 earnings reveal leadership test in downturn

LGI Homes posted higher Q3 2026 revenue and improved gross margin while cutting SG&A dollars. Demand weakened materially, with orders down 61.2% and cancellations up, putting focus on leadership, culture, and capital discipline.  AI Summary

A peculiar phenomenon in homebuilding has fascinated me for much of the past two-plus decades.

In virtually every market, across almost every customer segment and price point, a handful of homebuilders consistently outperform competitors facing essentially the same business conditions.

They face the same mortgage rates, land and development costs, labor constraints, household purchasing-power challenges and regulatory obstacles. They work with essentially the same raw materials, including people, capital, building products, subcontractors and operating processes. Yet their results can differ dramatically, especially when business conditions turn difficult.

A decade or so ago, a highly regarded homebuilding business strategist mused aloud to me about this phenomenon. He was struck by how companies dealt with essentially the same competitive hand, yet a few outlier leaders figured out how to produce better results than the rest.

I’ve thought about that observation often, particularly during periods when the industry’s cyclical pressures expose the difference between companies that can withstand adversity and those that can turn adversity into an opportunity to strengthen their businesses.

The distinction is especially relevant now. U.S. homebuilders are facing an unforgiving mix of weak selling conditions, elevated capital costs, stubbornly high land and development expenses, and households whose purchasing power has failed to keep pace with the cost of homeownership. These pressures have persisted long enough to strain business plans based on more favorable assumptions, and little is certain about when conditions will improve.

Which brings us to LGI Homes, its Q3 2026 earnings report, and a question that extends well beyond a single company’s quarterly performance:

What distinguishes homebuilding enterprises whose leaders and organizations can emerge from a prolonged downturn stronger than they entered it?

LGI Homes’ November 3 earnings report is a useful case study because its operating results show both encouraging evidence of management’s execution and unmistakable signs that the business faces tough sledding ahead.

The Woodlands, Texas-based builder reported 1,222 home closings in the third quarter, including 33 currently or previously leased homes, a 10.4% increase from the year-earlier quarter. Homebuilding revenues rose 10.3% to $437.5 million, and net income increased to $24.6 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with $19.7 million, or $0.85 per share, in the year-earlier quarter.

Profitability and expense management emerged as clear strengths. Homebuilding gross margin reached 20.2%, and adjusted homebuilding gross margin was 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 2.5% in absolute dollars, while SG&A as a percentage of total revenue improved 180 basis points year over year, reflecting operational rigor and executional excellence.

The company also reduced its net debt-to-capital ratio to 40.6%, up 420 basis points from a year earlier, and ended September with $447.7 million in liquidity. Its active community count increased by 7.1% year over year to 151.

Yet a forward-looking lens tells a far less rosy story. Net orders plunged 61.2% to 609 homes, down from 1,570 a year earlier, while the cancellation rate rose to 53.8% from 33.6%. Backlog declined 47.5% to 685 homes. Management narrowed its full-year closing guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reflecting weaker sales activity and ongoing affordability pressures.

These results speak of the vulnerability of LGI’s business model at a time when the company’s core customer is among the most financially constrained in the housing market.

LGI has built much of its business around helping renters become homeowners through a direct-to-consumer sales model, speculative construction, and a value proposition that emphasizes attainable monthly payments. These capabilities have helped distinguish the company for years. They also leave its sales performance especially vulnerable to turbulent headwinds, such as mortgage-rate movements and changes in buyer qualification.

The third-quarter numbers make it clear that LGI’s operational strengths have not shielded it from those pressures. Will the capabilities that helped the company develop its distinctive business model now enable it to adapt more effectively than competitors under the same conditions?

Wolfe Research’s November 3 assessment of LGI serves as an important counterweight to any temptation to interpret the company’s earnings performance as evidence that it has already mastered the current downturn.

Analyst Trevor Allinson and his team credited LGI’s Q3 operating performance, namely its gross-margin strength and SG&A expense reductions, while maintaining a Peer Perform rating. Wolfe noted that LGI’s predominantly self-developed land position supports margins at a time when several competitors have sustained hits to sequential margins.

Wolf Research’s analysis also explicitly recognizes LGI’s process-driven organization as a competitive strength, citing the company’s ability to pare back operating errors in land acquisition, construction efficiency and warranty management.

This is not to say that Wall Street exactly overlooks the value of management execution or organizational capability. Wolfe’s analysis shows that analysts recognize those strengths and attempt to account for their financial impact. What’s hard to quantify is how much those muscle-memory operational capabilities can influence future results when demand remains both tepid and unpredictable.

Wolfe’s assessment highlights that LGI’s order decline creates a difficult trade-off between sales pace and profitability. With third-quarter net order absorption averaging about 1.3 homes per community per month, the company faces pressure to accelerate sales, potentially through additional incentives that would erode margins.

The firm reduced its 2027 earnings-per-share estimate by 30.1%, from $3.42 to $2.39, reflecting its expectation that weaker demand and the need to balance price against sales volume will constrain profitability. Its concerns also extend to LGI’s leverage, its comparatively high SG&A expense ratio, and its substantial owned-land position, all of which can weigh on returns when inventory turnover slows.

Those financial risks aren’t merely temporary obstacles that a strong corporate culture can surmount through resolve.

LGI’s net debt-to-capital ratio of 40.6% remains elevated relative to many competitors, despite recent improvements. Its 50,270 owned lots represent a substantial capital commitment, especially given current sales rates.

The company therefore enters the next phase of this downturn with meaningful strengths, but also with structural exposures that could constrain its flexibility if weak demand persists.

In a conversation earlier this week, Tony Avila, founder of Builder Advisor Group and Avila Real Estate Capital, offered a useful framework for identifying homebuilders best positioned to weather and grow stronger in the current environment.

Avila cited stronger margins, lower leverage, attractive finished-lot positions, higher returns on capital, and the ability to serve a broader range of buyers as key indicators of financial strength. Geographic diversification can provide additional protection, although builders operating in individual markets with favorable supply-and-demand dynamics may also be well positioned.

His observations reflect a reality that homebuilding’s financial fundamentals become especially important when market conditions deteriorate and access to capital becomes more expensive or more restrictive. Builders with stronger balance sheets and favorable land positions can preserve liquidity, maintain operational flexibility, and pursue opportunities that weaker competitors may be forced to abandon.

Avila also cautioned that the industry’s current difficulties could persist into 2028, suggesting that the ability to withstand a prolonged period of weak demand may become an increasingly important competitive distinction.

These characteristics provide an essential foundation for evaluating resilience. They identify which companies have the financial capacity to withstand adversity and retain strategic options while competitors face mounting constraints.

I would argue that they represent the table stakes of resilience rather than its full measure.

Financial strength can give an enterprise room to maneuver, but it does not necessarily indicate whether management will recognize changing opportunities, make the right adjustments, or mobilize its organization to perform better.

By the same token, a company that falls short of some of these financial criteria may possess organizational capabilities that enable it to improve its position over time, provided its financial constraints do not undermine those efforts.

For LGI, its land holdings and leverage are sources of financial risk, yet its operating history and recent management decisions suggest an organization actively attempting to adapt rather than simply waiting for market conditions to improve.

At the recent HousingWire Homebuilder Summit in Dallas, I introduced a framework for evaluating the organizational qualities that distinguish homebuilding enterprises capable of sustained improvement.

I described five interdependent characteristics: Character. Capability. Collaboration. Competitive fire. And customer-first culture.

Together, they form what I think of as a leadership stack, analogous to the technology stack, the capital stack, or a coordinated network of subcontractors that supports other essential elements of a homebuilding business.

Character builds the trust that enables leaders and teams to confront difficult realities and make decisions that serve the enterprise’s long-term interests. Capability reflects the organization’s accumulated knowledge, skills, and ability to execute, while collaboration enables people across functions and markets to learn from one another and solve problems more effectively.

Competitive fire fuels the determination to improve performance rather than accept prevailing conditions as an excuse for disappointing results. A customer-first culture keeps the entire organization focused on delivering homes and experiences that people genuinely need, value, and can afford.

These qualities are not substitutes for sound financial management. Their value lies in how they influence the decisions, processes and behaviors that ultimately drive financial results.

Nor can they be established simply through executive declarations about corporate culture. More convincing evidence comes from what leaders and their organizations actually do when prior assumptions break apart.

LGI’s predominantly owned and self-developed land position has long been central to its operating model. By keeping much of the land development process in-house, the company has sought to manage lot costs, maintain product consistency, and preserve margins that might otherwise be surrendered to third-party developers.

During the earnings call, Chairman and CEO Eric Lipar emphasized the importance of the strategy.

“Our on-balance sheet predominantly owned land strategy, together with our in-house development capabilities reflects the long-term decisions we’ve made to set LGI apart from much of the industry. It remains a competitive advantage, generating strong margins while giving us flexibility to adapt to changing market conditions.”

LGI’s Q3 margin performance reflects these advantages. However, the risks of tying up capital in land become more pronounced when demand slows and projected absorption rates prove overly optimistic.

Management has reduced its owned-lot position for six consecutive quarters, from a peak of 61,893 lots in the second quarter of 2022 to 50,270 as of September 30, 2026. Meanwhile, controlled lots increased 18.1% sequentially to 8,130, reflecting opportunities to pursue finished-lot takedowns and smaller projects that meet the company’s current underwriting requirements.

These adjustments do not transform LGI into an asset-light builder, nor do they eliminate the financial consequences of its current land investments. They do, however, demonstrate a willingness to adjust capital commitments while preserving the capabilities that have historically differentiated its business.

CFO Charles Merdian offered another example during the earnings call, explaining that the company has adjusted the size and timing of future development sections to reflect slower absorption assumptions.

Those tactics involve altering project execution, even after initial land acquisitions and infrastructure investments. Management cannot recover all previously committed capital, but it can adjust the timing and amount of additional investment required to bring future lots to market.

This is organizational adaptability expressed through capital allocation and operational execution. It reflects the capacity to revisit assumptions, coordinate decisions across land development and construction functions, and change course without necessarily abandoning the underlying strategy.

LGI’s speculative construction and direct-to-consumer sales model offers another example of the distinction between adapting an operating strategy and abandoning its core customer proposition.

The company has historically focused on renters and first-time buyers whose purchasing decisions depend heavily on affordable monthly payments and the ability to move into a completed home on a relatively predictable schedule.

That positioning has become more challenging as mortgage rates and household expenses have tightened qualification standards. LGI’s elevated cancellation rate and sharp decline in orders indicate that its core customers are struggling to convert interest in homeownership into completed transactions.

Yet Lipar’s comments suggest management views the company’s customer knowledge and operating specialization as reasons to maintain its basic approach while modifying the supporting processes.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership, and our job is to remain disciplined while adapting our sales and financing strategies, production plans and product offering to current conditions.”

The company has expanded its sales process to accommodate buyers who need more time to qualify, while using closing-cost assistance, mortgage-rate buydowns and forward rate commitments to improve payment affordability. Management has also emphasized the need to adjust production plans and product offerings without sacrificing the features and customer experience that support the company’s value proposition.

These measures cannot eliminate the underlying affordability problem. Their effectiveness will depend on whether enough prospective customers can ultimately qualify and close at prices that maintain acceptable returns.

But they illustrate the strategic value of an organization that understands its customers well enough to adapt how it serves them while remaining committed to the needs that originally shaped its business model.

In this context, a customer-first culture becomes more than a statement of corporate values. It becomes a source of operating intelligence that informs decisions on financing, product, inventory, and the allocation of sales resources.

Of the five characteristics in the leadership stack, competitive fire may be the hardest to measure and the easiest to misunderstand or even overlook.

It is not merely optimism about an eventual market recovery, an appetite for expansion, or an unwillingness to acknowledge deteriorating conditions. Competitive fire becomes a meaningful organizational advantage when it fosters a persistent determination to improve performance while maintaining the discipline needed to protect the enterprise.

Founded in 2003, the company gained much of its early operating experience during the period surrounding the Great Financial Crisis, when collapsing housing demand, restricted credit and widespread industry failures forced homebuilders to reconsider fundamental assumptions about their businesses.

LGI emerged from that period and later expanded into a national homebuilder operating in 36 markets across 21 states. The company reports that it has earned a profit every year since its founding, a record that spans both the financial crisis and the industry’s more recent cycles of disruption.

That history does not establish that LGI will outperform during the current downturn. The industry’s competitive environment, capital structures, and affordability challenges have changed substantially since the GFC.

It does, however, suggest the company has developed institutional familiarity with adversity and a management culture shaped by operating without favorable market conditions. Its current community expansion strategy will be a significant test of that culture.

LGI expects to end 2027 with more than 180 active communities, approximately 20% above its third-quarter 2026 count. Management says much of the capital needed to support those openings has already been invested, allowing the company to expand its selling capacity without taking on incremental debt specifically to fund the openings.

At the same time, management expects the new communities to achieve absorption rates and margins similar to those currently seen, rather than assuming an imminent recovery in buyer demand. LGI is positioning itself for greater market reach while attempting to underwrite growth against the difficult conditions it observes, not the more favorable conditions it might prefer.

The strategy carries substantial execution risk. Expanding into more communities does not automatically translate into stronger earnings or higher returns when the pool of qualified buyers is constrained, and additional operating capacity can become a financial burden if sales productivity remains weak.

Still, the decision reflects an effort to preserve future growth opportunities while aligning investment and production plans with current market realities. Whether competitive fire becomes a genuine advantage will depend on how effectively LGI’s leadership and team execute those plans, learn from setbacks, and improve results in the coming quarters.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s concept of antifragility offers a useful way to frame the distinction between companies that merely survive adversity and those that become stronger because of it.

Resilience is the ability to absorb shocks, withstand disruption, and recover. Antifragility goes further, describing systems that benefit from volatility, stress, and uncertainty rather than merely enduring them.

Now, homebuilding is inherently cyclical, capital-intensive, and exposed to forces beyond the control of even its most capable executives. A resilient homebuilder may retain enough financial strength to weather a prolonged downturn and resume growth when demand improves. An antifragile homebuilder would use that same period to improve its processes, strengthen its people, sharpen its understanding of customers, and develop competitive advantages that leave it better positioned than before.

A single quarter of improved margins or successful cost reductions cannot establish the difference. It requires evidence that the organization has turned difficult experience into durable improvements in performance and competitive capability.

LGI has not yet demonstrated that outcome in the current cycle, but it has shown a willingness to adapt key elements of its operating model while preserving the strategic capabilities that management believes distinguish the company. Its land development adjustments, inventory management, sales-process changes and disciplined approach to balancing margins against volume provide observable evidence of that effort.

The next several quarters will show whether those decisions can improve absorption rates, cash generation, returns on capital, and competitive position, particularly if the industry’s difficult demand conditions persist through 2027 and beyond.

The industry’s current challenges are likely to produce meaningful differences in performance among homebuilders that appear superficially similar in their geographic exposure, customer segments and product offerings.

Homebuilding’s outliers are not necessarily the companies that begin a downturn with the strongest balance sheets, the most favorable markets, or the fewest obstacles. Those advantages matter enormously, but they do not fully explain why certain competitors consistently outperform.

The more elusive advantage lies in how organizations use their resources, learn from changing conditions, and translate leadership into sustained operational improvement.

That is where competitive fire – the determination that drives an organization to keep finding ways to improve when headwinds make improvement hardest – plays a role in homebuilding business outcomes that’s all too unappreciated.

#5492. Ballot roulette: Florida voters pick property tax break over local services

Florida voters approved a homestead exemption expansion with 62% support, with increases to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Opponents warned of public safety and service impacts, and state analysts projected nearly $5 billion in lost local revenue in 2027-28.  AI Summary

With the cost of living on the ballot, Florida voters approved a major tax break for homeowners.

The amendment to increase the Sunshine State’s homestead exemption won the 60% it needed on election night. Voters weren’t swayed by warnings that the higher exemption would devastate municipal coffers and services.

The ballot measure was given little chance of winning. But current economic conditions proved an insurmountable obstacle for the argument against the measure.

Unofficial returns showed it finishing with 62% of the vote. The changes take effect in phases starting in 2027.

“An incredible victory for Florida homeowners!” the Florida Republican Party wrote on social media. “More money stays in your pocket.”

Neil Schiller, managing partner at Government Law Group, told HousingWire TBD the result will change how cities weigh development.

“Projects that generate jobs, economic activity, and alternative tax revenues may become more attractive, while developments that require significant public services and infrastructure will face greater financial scrutiny,” Schiller said. “Amendment 3 may be remembered as the moment Florida cities had to fundamentally reinvent how they do business.”

The vote shows how important affordability has become, Andrew Hellinger, co-principal at Urban-X Group, developer of River Landing Shops & Residences in Miami, said in an e-mail to HousingWire TBD.

Hellinger added, “However, people still need roads, public transportation and essential community services, and those have to be paid for.”

The amendment replaces the $50,000 homestead exemption with a phased increase. It rises to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Only primary residences qualify, so second-home and investment-property owners get nothing.

Homeowners must establish Florida residency by Dec. 31, 2026, to get the full benefit. Later arrivals get the $50,000 exemption for four years before qualifying. The school board levy is excluded.

The measure also cuts the annual assessment cap on non-homestead commercial property from 10% to 5%. That change starts Jan. 1, 2027. Renters, who occupy about a third of Florida’s housing units, get no relief.

Gov. Ron DeSantis called a special session to put the amendment on the ballot. Lawmakers approved it with changes protecting school funding. DeSantis had sought a broader exemption.

DeSantis cast the measure as a fix for tax bills inflated by pandemic-era migration. Newcomers, led by New Yorkers, overwhelmed the housing supply and lifted values and tax burdens for longtime residents. Florida home prices rose more than 50% between 2020 and 2022.

Prices have since stalled, and the average home value fell 3.7% over the past year. Assessments haven’t followed: under the Save Our Homes recapture rule, they keep rising until they meet market value. The annual increase is capped at 3% or inflation, whichever is less.

Most counties held millage rates steady or cut them, yet bills still climbed. City tax bills statewide rose about 50% on average over several years.

The Florida Sheriffs Association said in August it was “significantly concerned.” By mid-September, it was running ads featuring sheriffs from four counties. One said, “We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it.”

Association President Billy Woods warned of fewer deputies, slower 911 response and more crime. Opponents also included the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association. The Florida League of Cities and Florida Association of Counties opposed it, citing too much uncertainty.

According to the legislature’s economic research office, estimated local governments would lose nearly $5 billion in 2027-28.

The Florida Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, created Floridians for Shared Prosperity, which sponsored a campaign urging a no vote.

“Amendment 3 will leave working families and seniors with a lose-lose choice: pay more through new fees and higher taxes or face major cuts to the services you depend on,” the campaign’s website stated.

Voters approved the amendment anyway, with encouragement from the Florida Realtors and others in real estate.

“This is your one shot at real property tax relief,” apartment owner and investor Grant Washington wrote on social media Monday. “Vote Yes on Amendment 3 and put your money back where it belongs. In your pocket!”

#5491. Algorized Presents AFM at CIIE 2026 in Shanghai: The Foundation Model That Gives Machines an Understanding of People, Across Industries

One model for robots, buildings and devices, running live at CIIE on data from a single standard wireless sensor.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Foundation models gave machines an understanding of language and images. The Algorized Foundation Model (AFM) gives them an understanding of people. Algorized, a global company developing a foundation model, presents Algorized Foundation Model (AFM) at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE 2026) in Shanghai from 5 to 10 November. Algorized takes part as an invited guest in the start-up exhibition area hosted by BMW Technology Office China.

Algorized was identified by BMW Technology Office China through its outside-in scouting activities because of the company's distinctive offering in human-aware perception for Physical AI. The invitation to present at CIIE 2026 provides visibility and an opportunity for technology exchange. Participation alone does not mean that any collaboration with BMW exists or that BMW endorses or validates Algorized's technology. AFM and every statement in this release about its capabilities are Algorized's own.

Algorized's research began with a search-and-rescue question: can a wireless signal find a heartbeat in earthquake rubble? That work grew into a foundation model for everyday settings. Robot arms and mobile robots now share floors with workers, buildings respond to their occupants, and connected devices react to presence and activity. Each has typically had its own perception system, built for one task. Algorized builds the understanding of people once, as a foundation model that every new product can start from.

AFM works from standard Wi-Fi, UWB or mmWave sensors and runs at the edge, on the device itself. The sensor sends out low-power wireless signals that pass through clothing and reflect off the body. From those reflections, AFM tells a person from an object, locates and tracks each person in real time, and picks up the sub-millimeter chest movements that come with each breath and heartbeat. It perceives people through darkness, smoke and dust, and runs across sensor types and silicon platforms, so robot, machine and device makers can build on one perception foundation.

The applications run across industries. China installed 354,000 industrial robots in 2025, 59% of all installations worldwide, according to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) World Robotics 2026 report. In robotics and production, AFM makes a robot arm or a mobile robot aware of the people around it, so it can adapt its speed and path while workers share the floor. Sense, anticipate, adapt. In smart buildings, the same model senses presence and people count, so heating, ventilation and cooling can follow actual occupancy. In connected devices, it turns breathing and heart rate into non-diagnostic well-being features.

On the stand, AFM runs live on data from one standard wireless sensor. As a visitor walks up, AFM classifies them as a person and tracks them in real time. A simulated robot arm adjusts its speed to their distance, waits when they come close and resumes its task as they step back. A visitor who stands still sees their breathing and heart rate on screen. Visitors and press can find Algorized at the BMW booth and can book meetings through the Algorized media contact below.

"Everyone assumes we built five models. We built one, and every machine that works around people can build on it. Being selected by BMW for the CIIE 2026 showcase lets us show it live in China, the world's largest market for industrial robots," said Natalya Lopareva, CEO and founder of Algorized.

Algorized builds the edge-native nervous system for Physical AI. One foundation model senses human presence, vital signs, motion, and intent through occlusion - delivering real-time human-aware perception from standard wireless sensors, where cameras and light-based systems go blind. The model ships as two products: a foundation model stack embedded on partner silicon across automotive, spaces, and industrial applications, and a quality-managed safety stack for human-robot collaboration. Backed by the Amazon Industrial Innovation Fund and rooted in proprietary Swiss research, Algorized partners with silicon manufacturers and industrial OEMs across robotics, automotive, and smart spaces. Learn more at www.algorized.com.

Robots working beside people need a reliable estimate of human movement. Their controllers also need to know how far they can trust that estimate....

#5489. Cyber ups and downs: Datadog falls 14% on outlook tied to one customer as Rapid7 jumps and Fastly slides

Datadog Inc., Rapid7 Inc. and Fastly Inc. all beat Wall Street’s third-quarter forecasts today, but Rapid7 was the only one of the three to see its shares rise.

A cautious outlook tied to one large customer knocked about 14% off Datadog’s stock in regular trading. Rapid7 jumped 18% after hours on results that came despite a decline in revenue.

For its third quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Datadog reported adjusted earnings of 81 cents per share, up from 55 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 64 cents per share on revenue of $1.14 billion.

Unadjusted net income climbed to $118.3 million from $33.9 million, and the adjusted operating margin widened five points to 28%. Billings in the quarter rose 30% to $1.16 billion, Chief Financial Officer David Obstler said on the earnings call, with remaining performance obligations up 38% at $3.85 billion. Free cash flow came to $251 million.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Olivier Pomel told analysts that more than 850 artificial intelligence companies now use Datadog, roughly 100 more than at the end of June. Adoption is strong across the platform as customers scale “their digital operations and use of AI,” he said in the earnings release. Customers worth $100,000 or more a year in recurring revenue rose 20% to about 4,860.

Full-year guidance went up. Datadog now expects 2026 revenue of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion, against the $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion it projected in August, and adjusted earnings of $2.73 to $2.75 per share. Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are forecast at 69 to 71 cents per share.

Revenue for the fourth quarter is guided at $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly what analysts had expected, with the top of the range only about $3 million above third-quarter revenue. The forecast assumes Datadog’s largest customer, an AI provider the company has not named, spends no more than its contractual minimum, according to Obstler.

Usage on that account dropped in the third quarter while staying above the floor. Excluding it, implied fourth-quarter growth is in the low- to mid-30% range. Early renewals with some large AI customers, signed at higher commitments in return for better pricing, are also holding back near-term revenue.

The roughly 14% drop today made it two straight quarters in which a beat failed to hold up the stock. Datadog shares closed 19% lower in August, the day the company disclosed the customer’s planned cutback.

In Rapid7’s third quarter, also ended Sept. 30, the cybersecurity company posted adjusted earnings of 60 cents per share, up from 57 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $212.4 million, down 2.5% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 46 cents per share on revenue of $209 million.

Annualized recurring revenue slipped 2.2%, to $819.7 million, ahead of the roughly $812 million the company had guided to in August. Adjusted operating income rose to $46.2 million from $36.9 million. Unadjusted net income fell to $3.5 million from $9.8 million after $10 million in restructuring costs from the 12% workforce cut announced in August and a $5.5 million write-down on a strategic equity investment.

Rapid7 demonstrated its Agentic SOC at Black Hat USA in August, using AI agents to speed up investigations while leaving high-impact decisions to analysts. Wael Mohamed, who took over as CEO in June, said the core business “is becoming more stable” and that “one quarter of stability is just a start.” Rapid7 is “not declaring victory,” he added.

The company’s full-year adjusted earnings forecast moved to $1.94 to $1.96 per share, well above the $1.78 to $1.83 it gave three months ago. Revenue guidance edged up to $841 million to $843 million. For the fourth quarter, Rapid7 sees revenue of $208 million to $210 million, down 3% to 4% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of 53 to 55 cents per share.

The stock climbed about 18% in extended trading.

Edge cloud platform provider Fastly reported adjusted earnings of 17 cents per share for its third quarter, up from 7 cents a year earlier, on record revenue of $190.2 million, up 20% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 12 cents per share on revenue of $187.9 million.

Most of Fastly’s revenue still comes from network services, which grew 16%, to $138 million. Security sales rose twice as fast, to $44.7 million, in a quarter when the company also launched AI Firewall to block prompt injection and other attacks before they reach a model. Trailing-12-month net retention was its highest since 2022, at 119%. The top 10 customers now account for 39% of revenue, up from 32% a year ago.

Fourth-quarter revenue is forecast at $198 million to $202 million, ahead of the $197 million analysts had modeled. Full-year revenue guidance moved up to $744 million to $748 million from $732 million to $746 million in August. Adjusted earnings for 2026 are now expected at 61 to 63 cents per share. None of that stopped Fastly shares from falling about 14% after the bell.

#5488. What housing market headlines can’t tell your clients

National housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing, but local market conditions tell a more nuanced story. HousingWire Data shows diverging trends between Houston and its broader metro, rising inventory and pricing pressure in Phoenix, and changing inventory patterns in Tampa. Interactive HousingWire Intelligence charts help housing professionals identify emerging shifts and translate market data into actionable guidance for buyers and sellers.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates are moving closer to 7%, and housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing. But what does that mean for a homeowner preparing to list, a buyer wondering whether to wait or an agent trying to set realistic expectations?

In his latest Housing Market Tracker, HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami explains why a path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table. While weekly pending home sales have recently stabilized, that doesn’t yet signal a sustained recovery.

For housing professionals, the opportunity is to translate those national trends into what clients are experiencing in their own markets.

HousingWire Data from Houston, Phoenix and Tampa reveals three things worth watching:

A client sees that housing demand is stabilizing and asks whether it’s finally a good time to sell.

Houston demonstrates why the answer requires more local context.

Across the Houston metro, the ratio of new pending sales to new listings improved during October, but not because buyer activity increased. New listings declined faster than pending sales, making the ratio look stronger even as fewer homes went under contract.

Within Houston city limits, the opposite happened. Pending sales declined faster than new listings, pushing the ratio lower.

Even inventory told a different story. Active inventory was higher than a year ago across the metro but lower within the city.

Neither market showed growing pending activity, yet the conditions affecting buyers and sellers were different.

For a homeowner, that distinction matters more than whether a regional headline describes the market as improving.

The takeaway: Use broader housing trends to start the conversation, then show clients what’s happening among the homes they’re actually competing with. A seller needs to understand current competition and buyer activity, not simply whether the overall market appears stronger.

A homeowner considering whether to wait for lower mortgage rates might assume that more affordable financing will bring more buyers.

But lower rates could also encourage more sellers to list, making the relationship between supply and demand especially important.

Phoenix illustrates what happens when several indicators point in the same direction.

Over the latest four-week period, new pending sales declined faster than new listings. Compared with a year ago, pending activity was down nearly 17%, while new listings were slightly higher.

Meanwhile, active inventory continued to grow, and more than half of active listings had experienced a price reduction.

Together, those indicators suggest increasing competition among sellers. Fewer homes are moving into pending status, more inventory is available and price reductions are becoming more prevalent.

That doesn’t guarantee prices will fall, but it identifies conditions that could create additional pricing pressure if the trend continues.

The takeaway: Don’t evaluate pending sales, inventory or price reductions in isolation. When several indicators reinforce one another, they provide stronger evidence of where conditions may be headed. That can help sellers evaluate pricing and timing, while giving buyers a clearer picture of their negotiating position.

A seller points out that inventory is still lower than last year. Does that mean competition remains limited?

Tampa shows why the direction of recent activity matters just as much as the year-over-year comparison.

Within Tampa city limits, new listings and pending sales were essentially unchanged over the latest four weeks. Active inventory remained below last year’s level, and the share of listings with price reductions had declined.

But inventory was also beginning to increase compared with the preceding four weeks.

That doesn’t establish a market shift. Recent pending activity has been relatively steady, and price-cut share continues to ease. Still, the inventory increase is worth monitoring.

If inventory continues building while pending activity remains weak, sellers could face greater competition even before the year-over-year inventory comparison turns positive.

Try it yourself: Switch the chart above between 6M and YoY. The six-month view shows how inventory has been building recently, while the year-over-year comparison reveals that inventory remains below last year’s levels. Both are true, but each tells you something different about the market.The takeaway: A favorable market statistic doesn’t mean conditions are standing still. Track recent changes alongside year-over-year trends, and revisit pricing or buying strategies when the evidence begins to shift.

Logan’s Housing Market Tracker provides the national context. HousingWire Intelligence helps professionals connect that context to the markets where their clients are making decisions.

Use HousingWire Intelligence to chart new listings, pending sales, active inventory and price reductions in your city. Look at how the indicators move together over time, compare recent changes with the same period last year and consider what those patterns mean for the properties your clients are buying or selling.

Your clients can find national headlines and AI-generated market summaries on their own. What they need from you is the expertise to explain what those trends mean for their home, their competition and their next decision.

Methodology: HousingWire Data analysis of single-family homes across all price quartiles for the four weeks ending Oct. 30, 2026, compared with the preceding four weeks and the equivalent period in 2025. City-level figures are used for Houston, Phoenix and Tampa, with Houston metro data included for comparison. New listings and pending sales are four-week totals; inventory and price-cut shares are averages of weekly snapshots. Price-cut share represents active listings that have experienced a reduction, not reductions made during the reporting period.

Adjusted EBITDA  (Non-GAAP Financial Measure)

Adjusted EBITDA is defined as net income plus interest expense, less interest income and other gain (loss) recognized on investments, plus income tax expense, and plus depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), as adjusted for (i) contributions to private Arizona school tuition organizations in lieu of the payment of state income taxes; (ii) share-based compensation; and (iii) unusual charges or gains, such as litigation and regulatory costs, non-recurring costs, impairment charges and asset write-offs, severance costs, and exit or lease termination costs.  We present Adjusted EBITDA because we consider it to be an important supplemental measure of our operating performance.  We also make certain compensation decisions based, in part, on our operating performance, as measured by Adjusted EBITDA.  All of the adjustments made in our calculation of Adjusted EBITDA are adjustments to items that management does not consider to be reflective of our core operating performance.  Management considers our core operating performance to be that which can be affected by our managers in any particular period through their management of the resources that affect our underlying revenue and profit generating operations during that period and does not consider the items for which we make adjustments (as listed above) to be reflective of our core performance.

We believe Adjusted EBITDA allows us to compare our current operating results with corresponding historical periods and with the operational performance of other companies in our industry because it does not give effect to potential differences caused by variations in capital structures (affecting relative interest expense, including the impact of write-offs of deferred financing costs when companies refinance their indebtedness), tax positions (such as the impact on periods or companies of changes in effective tax rates or net operating losses), the book amortization of intangibles (affecting relative amortization expense), and other items that we do not consider reflective of underlying operating performance.  We also present Adjusted EBITDA because we believe it is frequently used by securities analysts, investors, and other interested parties as a measure of performance.

In evaluating Adjusted EBITDA, investors should be aware that in the future we may incur expenses similar to the adjustments described above.  Our presentation of Adjusted EBITDA should not be construed as an inference that our future results will be unaffected by expenses that are unusual, non-routine, or non-recurring.  Adjusted EBITDA has limitations as an analytical tool in that, among other things, it does not reflect:

In addition, other companies, including other companies in our industry, may calculate these measures differently than we do, limiting the usefulness of Adjusted EBITDA as a comparative measure.  Because of these limitations, Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered as a substitute for net income, operating income, or any other performance measure derived in accordance with and reported under GAAP, or as an alternative to cash flow from operating activities or as a measure of our liquidity.  We compensate for these limitations by relying primarily on our GAAP results and only use Adjusted EBITDA as a supplemental performance measure.

#5486. Bright turns on Ocusell integration so agents enter listings once

Bright MLS launched a live integration with Ocusell’s network, letting agents enter and edit listings once and syndicate to Bright and other MLSs. Ocusell says it can cut listing creation time up to 75% and prevent over 85% of compliance errors.  AI Summary

Bright MLS has turned on its live integration with Ocusell’s listing network, allowing brokers and agents who work across multiple MLSs in the Mid-Atlantic to enter and edit listings once and syndicate them into Bright and other participating MLSs without double data entry, the companies announced Tuesday.

The operational launch marks the first major product milestone from the joint venture Bright and Ocusell formed in 2025 and introduces OneList, a co-developed listing input platform built on the Ocusell Network that is designed to give brokerages and MLSs a single, connected listing interface nationwide.

“We entered into this joint venture to remove friction from the daily work of our brokers and agents,” said Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan, who is also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner. “Our role as an MLS is to adapt to how real estate pros operate and to help them succeed. This partnership with Ocusell is a clear example of that.”

The launch comes as the Open Real Estate (ORE) initiative is running a national request for proposal search for a vendor that can deliver “input once, distribute everywhere” listing entry across markets. Ocusell says it is already live across 30 MLSs, and with OneList now operating at Bright, one of the nation’s largest MLSs, the company is positioning its network as a scalable solution for multi-MLS entry.

For brokers, the integration is aimed at reducing staff time and compliance risk tied to re-keying listing data into separate MLS systems. Agents can enter listing specifics, photos and disclosures once; the platform then auto-validates those fields against each local MLS’s rules while maintaining existing access and display policies. According to Ocusell, its infrastructure can cut listing creation time by up to 75% and prevent more than 85% of compliance errors.

On top of cross-market sync, according to the announcement, the forthcoming OneList interface layers in real-time AI-driven compliance and Fair Housing screening, intelligent media management with automated photo tagging and organization, and integrated listing promotion that lets agents launch targeted marketing campaigns from the listing input workflow.

“This is a total game changer for agents, brokers, and home buyers and sellers,” said Steve Mapes, executive in charge of growth strategy at Bright MLS. “When agents aren’t stuck doing double data entry because they belong to multiple MLSs, they have more time to serve their clients and do what they do best. Technology should make things better, faster and more efficient, and we’re excited to get this up and running.”

“Now is the time for MLSs to help shape what comes next for their brokers,” Hayden Rieveschl, the CEO of Ocusell and a 2026 HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “Bright and Ocusell are demonstrating what’s possible when you listen to brokers and turn their needs into action. As more brokerages operate across markets, MLSs have an opportunity to remove barriers and make doing business easier.”

The move reflects a broader shift in organized real estate as large regional brokerages, teams and franchises increasingly span multiple MLS territories while regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys scrutinize how listing data is shared and displayed.

For brokers and agents, multi-MLS input has historically meant duplicate work, inconsistent data, higher error rates and delays getting listings in front of buyers across markets. A centralized entry layer like OneList, if widely adopted, could streamline operations for multi-market firms, tighten compliance controls and create more standardized listing data for downstream tools, portals and valuation models.

For MLS organizations, the Bright-Ocusell rollout is a signal that listing input may increasingly be handled through connected, vendor-operated platforms rather than bespoke MLS-only interfaces, potentially reshaping how MLSs think about technology procurement, interoperability and data licensing.

Ocusell said the integration is live now for active Bright MLS brokerages that manage listings across multiple markets, according to the announcement. Bright said rollout timelines and early-access details for the broader OneList platform will be shared in future communications.

#5485. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5483. Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep

Shares of Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. closed higher today following Democrats’ resounding midterm victory.

Amazon jumped 8.3% at one point and ended the trading session 6.1% higher than Tuesday. Microsoft gained nearly 6.7% while Alphabet and Google rose by about 3.1% and 1.4%, respectively. Multiple industry analysts tied the stock gains to the companies’ artificial intelligence buildout.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on a campaign that emphasized data center restrictions. Furthermore, voters approved 40 ballot measures focused on blocking or limiting AI infrastructure projects. Bloomberg cited Robert Pavlik, a senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, as saying that tech giants’ shares jumped because investors believe a data center slowdown could improve their finances.

Amazon, Meta and Google have become cash-flow-negative in recent months because of their steep infrastructure investments. Last Wednesday, the search giant reported a negative cash flow that exceeded the consensus estimate by about $6.4 billion. Google’s stock price plummeted 10% in after-hours trading even though its cloud revenue more than doubled.

Needham & Co., B. ‌Riley ⁠Wealth and prominent tech industry analyst Ben Thompson highlighted another possible contributor to the stock rally. New restrictions on AI projects would make computing infrastructure more scarce, which would boost the value of existing data centers. That would benefit the tech giants that logged share price gains today.

Thompson noted that neoclouds, or emerging AI-focused cloud providers, may also benefit in certain respects. Developments for which they have already secured regulatory permission could become more valuable. At the same time, they may find it more difficult to finance new sites.

That dynamic weighed on chip stocks today. Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. both shed more than 3% of their value, while Broadcom Inc. declined 2%. SK hynix Inc., the world’s largest supplier of HBM memory for graphics cards, dropped by more than 5%. One notable exception was Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which ended the trading day about 1% higher.

Thompson noted that the midterms could also affect the AI industry in other ways. He pointed out that a stricter regulatory environment may give space-based data centers a boost. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, in turn, could see their hardware costs decline if new restrictions are placed on frontier model training. Such a development may ease their path to profitability.

Last month, Meta announced plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares to finance new data centers. On Monday, Oracle Corp. filed to issue $20 billion worth of bonds and shares in connection with its own AI buildout. It’s currently unclear how the midterm results will affect those initiatives and other large-scale data center projects currently underway.

#5482. Zillow pushes Preferred agent program toward 100% of buyer connections

Zillow reported Q3 2026 traffic down 3% to 215 million monthly users and a $158 million net loss. It highlighted AI mode expansion, Preferred growth and gains in mortgage and rentals revenue.  AI Summary

Zillow may be facing calls for investigations into some of its practices by consumer advocacy organizations and federal lawmakers, but the real estate listing portal giant is doubling down on its belief that it is “building the faster, easier and more affordable moving experience.”

“As more consumers and professionals use Zillow to move from dreaming to transacting, the old real estate experience will feel slow, difficult and expensive by comparison,”  Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman and Zillow COO and CFO Jeremy Hofmann wrote in a letter to shareholders published on Wednesday.

Despite this confidence, Zillow may be facing some headwinds. The company said that in the third quarter of 2026, visitor traffic to its apps and sites was down 3% during the quarter to 215 million average monthly unique users, while overall visits were down 5% annually to 2.3 billion according to Comscore data. Despite the declines, Comscore data shows that Zillow attracted 77% of average monthly unique visitors in the real estate category in Q3. In addition to this, the company said it has found that its AI search mode is deepening engagement, with visitors who use this option spending nearly three times as long as those who don’t on the site.

Zillow said that AI mode is now available to 100% of its signed-in users. The company said it was also exploring ways to use AI to make real estate professionals more productive and to help its internal engineers, who are using AI to ship 60% more changes to production than they did in 2024, according to Zillow.

“Buyers spend an average of two to three hours a week with us over about five months — and then for most, Zillow software and services power their transaction: the majority of residential real estate transactions in the U.S. run through our professional software,” the executives wrote. “Because of Zillow’s transaction infrastructure, our agentic AI does more than guide the shopping experience people love; it assists consumers and professionals throughout the transaction itself.

In addition to the decline in traffic, Zillow also reported a net loss of $158 million for the quarter, down from a $10 million net income generated in Q3 2025. This decline came even as revenue rose 7% annually to $724 million.

Zillow’s Preferred lead referral program is one of cornerstones of its revenue generation engine. The company reported that in Q3, two-thirds of buyer connections came to a Preferred agent partner in the integrated experience, roughly double what it was a year ago. Zillow said it was on track for Preferred to represent over three-quarters of connections by the end of the year, with it anticipating reaching 100% of connections in the first half of 2027. Zillow also noted that Preferred connections generate 35% more revenue per connection that its previous lead generation model.

Even with the growth of the Preferred program, Zillow’s for-sale revenue was flat year-over-year at $489 million. In addition to this, its residential segment recorded a 4% annual decline in revenue to $419 million, which the company attributed to higher-than-expected mortgage rates putting downward pressure on housing transaction volume.

Bright spots in Zillow’s Q3 earnings report occurred in its mortgage and rentals segments. Zillow’s mortgage rose 32% annually to $70 million, due to a 55% increase in purchase loan origination volume to $2.0 billion.

In markets where Zillow has integrated its mortgage product with its Preferred program the longest, Zillow said adoption rates of Zillow Home Loans is around 20%.

“We are also making Zillow Home Loans a trusted lender for Preferred agent partners’ entire book of business, not just for clients they connect with through Zillow,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

Rentals revenue was up 26% year-over-year to $220 million, which the company attributed to multifamily revenue growing 35% year over year. Zillow said its rentals segment now accounts for roughly 30% of its total revenue, up from 21% two years ago. Additionally, the company noted that 81,000 multifamily properties were advertised on Zillow at the end of the third quarter, a 17% annual increase.

“Diversifying into this space has brought us a large growth opportunity and made our business more robust,” the executives wrote. “Our rentals strategy is to offer the broadest, most comprehensive inventory from single-family homes to large apartment buildings, and to streamline the transaction experience for consumers and housing providers.”

Executives added that they believe Zillow is still just scratching the surface of the opportunity presented by the rentals sector.

“We see a clear path to more than $1 billion in annual rentals revenue and a substantial opportunity to keep growing across both multifamily and longtail rentals well beyond that milestone,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

The company also highlighted the performance of some of its other offerings, noting that its CRM product, Follow Up Boss, recorded roughly 141,000 monthly active users in Q3, up 16% annually. In addition to this, Zillow said over 800 brokerages had signed up for its pre-marketing product Zillow Preview and its listing enhancement product, Zillow Showcase, was on 5.4% of all new U.S. listings.

“Even as housing conditions deteriorated sharply, Zillow kept growing and outperforming, powered by our brand, audience, value to partners, disciplined cost management and strong growth levers across our well-diversified business,” Hofmann and Wacksman wrote. “These advantages are driving our performance through an exceptionally difficult macro environment today and position us to accelerate when conditions improve.”

PropWallet was designed to add value to the prop firm via continued customer engagement and to the prop trader via the receipt of additional value. The withdrawal is settled internally, with no processor fees involved, and its value returns to the operator in the form of future purchases.

At withdrawal, the trader selects PropWallet as the method, and the breakdown shows the bonus before anything is submitted.

For example, on a $500 payout at an 80/20 split, a trader receives $450 into his PropWallet instead of $400 in cash.

Once the payout is approved, the credit appears in the trader's dashboard as a credit and can be used for future purchases immediately.

At checkout, traders choose how much PropWallet credit to apply and can combine it with a discount code. Operators keep control of the feature. They can add or remove credit manually with a logged reason, which also makes PropWallet a great tool to support loyalty programs, membership programs and as a periodic incentive via cash drops into their PropWallet.
